questions.stem: In geography, a region is best defined as:
options: an area of land that has no human settlement
an area with shared features that set it apart
any area that is governed by a single local council
a country with a population of more than ten million
questions.explanation: Regions are defined by common physical or human features, such as a river basin, climate zone or economic area. Their boundaries may cross state or national borders.

questions.stem: The Murray-Darling Basin is defined as a region because it:
options: is the area of Australia with the highest rainfall and the most rainforest
follows the boundary of a single state, which manages all of its water
contains every irrigation farm in Australia and no other land uses
is the area drained by the Murray and Darling rivers and their tributaries
questions.explanation: The Basin is a drainage basin, so its boundary follows the watershed. It covers parts of Queensland, NSW, Victoria and South Australia and all of the ACT.

questions.stem: The Murray-Darling Basin covers about what share of Australia's land area?
options: about three-quarters
about one-seventh
about one-half
about one-fiftieth
questions.explanation: The Basin covers about 1 million km², roughly 14% of the continent, making it one of the largest river systems in Australia.

questions.stem: Rivers in the Murray-Darling Basin have some of the most variable flows of any large river system in the world. The main reason is:
options: a tropical climate with heavy rain in every month of the year
the absence of any dams, weirs or water extraction in the Basin
highly variable rainfall and high evaporation
constant snowmelt that keeps every river flowing at the same rate
questions.explanation: Much of the Basin is semi-arid, rainfall swings between drought and flood, and evaporation is high, so most rain never reaches the rivers. Flows naturally range from very low to major floods.

questions.stem: Which natural cycle has the strongest influence on wet and dry periods in the Murray-Darling Basin?
options: the 11-year sunspot cycle, which sets each year's rainfall
volcanic eruptions in New Zealand, which bring regular rain
ENSO: La Niña often brings floods, El Niño drought
the tides, which reverse the flow of the Darling every day
questions.explanation: La Niña events often bring above-average rainfall and floods to eastern Australia, while El Niño often brings drought. The Indian Ocean Dipole also affects the southern Basin.

questions.stem: River red gum forests on the Murray floodplains depend on periodic flooding. How have dams and water extraction affected them?
options: more frequent flooding has drowned most of the forests
dams have no effect because red gums never need floods
extraction has increased flooding, so forests have expanded
reduced flood frequency has stressed and killed many trees
questions.explanation: Regulation captures and diverts the moderate floods that once watered floodplain forests and wetlands, so many red gums have declined. Environmental water is now delivered to some sites.

questions.stem: During the Millennium Drought, the Murray Mouth needed continuous dredging and the Lower Lakes fell to very low levels. This is evidence of:
options: a purely natural change that would have happened without people
rising sea level flooding the Lower Lakes with seawater
too much rainfall in the upper catchment causing silt build-up
human-environment interaction: extraction plus drought
questions.explanation: Low rainfall combined with high levels of water diversion upstream meant too little water reached the sea to keep the mouth open. The change reflects both natural variability and human use.

questions.stem: Rice, cotton and almonds grown in the Basin are sold to buyers overseas, and water entitlements can be bought by investors, including foreign ones. This best shows:
options: the end of irrigated farming across the region
change in the region from international integration
the isolation of the region from global markets
the region's self-sufficiency in all food and water
questions.explanation: Global demand and prices shape which crops are grown and where water is used, and global capital invests in land and water. These links tie the Basin's land use to the world economy.

questions.stem: Mass fish kills occurred in the lower Darling River near Menindee in 2018-19 and in 2023. Which combination of factors best explains them?
options: salt water from the Southern Ocean flowing up the Darling
low flows, high temperatures and low dissolved oxygen
cold winter water and heavy snowfall in the upper catchment
too much water released from dams, flushing fish out to sea
questions.explanation: Low, still water in hot weather allowed algal blooms and, after events such as cool changes or floodwater carrying organic matter, oxygen levels crashed. Upstream extraction and drought both contributed to low flows.

questions.stem: The Murray-Darling Basin Plan, adopted in 2012 under the Water Act 2007, manages the Basin mainly by:
options: giving each state full control over water with no national rules
building new dams on every river to store all floodwater
setting sustainable limits on how much water is taken
banning all irrigation in the Basin and returning land to forest
questions.explanation: The Plan sets limits on consumptive water use and recovers water for the environment, through buybacks and infrastructure upgrades, to restore river health while supporting communities.

questions.stem: Irrigation communities argue that water buybacks harm local jobs, while downstream South Australia and environmental groups argue more water is needed for river health. In a regional study, this is best described as:
options: agreement among all groups on how to share water
a dispute that has no environmental dimension
a problem that affects only one state in the region
varying perspectives on managing a shared resource
questions.explanation: Upstream and downstream users, farmers and conservationists value water differently. The Basin crosses several jurisdictions, which makes cooperative management both necessary and difficult.

questions.stem: Climate projections suggest drier conditions and lower runoff in the southern Murray-Darling Basin. Which challenge does this pose for management?
options: less water to share among farms, towns and nature
more water than storages can hold in every future year
no change, because the Basin Plan fixes rainfall levels
an end to the need for environmental water in rivers
questions.explanation: Small falls in rainfall cause larger falls in runoff, so less water would be available for all users. This adds pressure to limits and allocations set under the Basin Plan.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show whether the Basin Plan has been effective in managing river health at one wetland site?
options: a single photograph of the wetland taken during a wet year
long-term monitoring of flows, bird breeding and vegetation
the number of newspaper articles written about the Basin Plan each year
the total amount of money spent on the Basin Plan across Australia
questions.explanation: Effectiveness is judged by outcomes at the site, such as more frequent watering, bird breeding and healthier vegetation, tracked over years that include both wet and dry periods.

questions.stem: Much of the Murray and lower Darling flows across very flat plains with a tiny gradient. Which characteristic of the rivers results?
options: short, steep rivers that reach the sea within days
rivers that freeze over completely every winter
slow flow, wide floodplains and long-lasting floods
fast flow through deep gorges with frequent waterfalls
questions.explanation: A very low gradient means water moves slowly and spreads across broad floodplains, so floods can take weeks or months to pass downstream. This shapes wetlands and settlement along the rivers.

questions.stem: Rising saline groundwater in parts of the Basin has raised river salinity. Salt interception schemes respond to this by:
options: adding fresh rainwater to the river from new coastal dams
planting crops that add salt to soils on the floodplain
releasing seawater into the river to dilute the salt
pumping saline groundwater away before it reaches the river
questions.explanation: Salt interception schemes pump salty groundwater to evaporation basins, keeping it out of the Murray. Revegetation and better irrigation practice also reduce the rise of saline water tables.

questions.stem: Warming since the mid-20th century has not been even across the globe. Which spatial pattern is observed?
options: the Southern Hemisphere has warmed while the north has cooled
land and the Arctic have warmed faster than average
the oceans have warmed faster than any land area on Earth
the equator has warmed much faster than the polar regions
questions.explanation: Land warms faster than ocean, and the Arctic has warmed several times faster than the global average, partly because of the ice-albedo feedback.

questions.stem: Which temporal characteristic of recent climate change is most significant?
options: its regular cycle of about 100 000 years like ice ages
its complete reversal every decade since the 1950s
its slow rate, which is far slower than any past change
its rapid rate compared with past natural changes
questions.explanation: Current warming is happening over decades, much faster than the natural shifts between glacial and interglacial periods, giving ecosystems and people little time to adapt.

questions.stem: Which is an impact of climate change on natural processes and systems?
options: a reduction in the frequency of extreme heat events
many species shifting their ranges poleward or uphill
a steady fall in sea level along most coastlines
an increase in the extent of Arctic sea ice in summer
questions.explanation: Warming is moving species' ranges poleward and to higher altitudes, changing the timing of events such as flowering, and causing coral bleaching. Sea level is rising and Arctic sea ice shrinking.

questions.stem: Rising sea levels and more intense storm surges threaten low-lying atoll nations such as Tuvalu and Kiribati. Which impact on people is most direct?
options: falling ocean temperatures killing commercial fish stocks
flooding and salt water entering groundwater and gardens
a shortage of land caused by volcanic uplift of the islands
colder winters reducing the growing season for crops
questions.explanation: Atolls are only a few metres above sea level, so flooding and saltwater intrusion damage homes, freshwater supplies and food crops, threatening long-term habitability.

questions.stem: Countries that have contributed least to greenhouse gas emissions, such as small Pacific island states, are often among the most affected by climate change. This raises the issue of:
options: the demographic transition in ageing countries
climate justice and who should bear the costs
the tragedy of the commons in local fisheries
urban sprawl on the fringes of large cities
questions.explanation: Climate justice concerns the unequal distribution of causes and impacts. It underpins calls for wealthy, high-emitting countries to fund adaptation and loss and damage in vulnerable countries.

questions.stem: A fossil fuel exporter, a Pacific island government and a renewable energy company may hold different views on how fast emissions should be cut. This illustrates:
options: a scientific disagreement about whether warming occurs
a local issue with no international dimension
varying perspectives shaped by different interests
full agreement among all groups on climate policy
questions.explanation: Economic interests, vulnerability and opportunities shape how groups view climate action. The science of warming is well established; the debate is mainly about responses.

questions.stem: Climate change mitigation refers to actions that:
options: help people cope with impacts that are already happening
rebuild communities after an extreme weather event
predict the weather accurately a few days in advance
cut greenhouse gas emissions or remove them from the air
questions.explanation: Mitigation tackles the cause by cutting emissions, for example through renewable energy, or by increasing carbon sinks such as forests. Adaptation deals with the impacts.

questions.stem: Which is an example of climate change adaptation?
options: switching a vehicle fleet from petrol to electric
breeding heat- and drought-tolerant crop varieties
replacing coal-fired power stations with solar farms
placing a price on carbon emissions from industry
questions.explanation: Adaptation reduces harm from changes that are occurring or expected, such as hotter, drier conditions for farming. The other options cut emissions, which is mitigation.

questions.stem: Why does the IPCC stress both the rate and the magnitude of future warming when discussing mitigation?
options: mitigation only affects the rate of warming, never how much warming finally occurs
slower warming always increases the total amount of warming that will eventually occur
faster, larger warming leaves less time to adapt and risks crossing tipping points
the rate of warming does not matter, as long as total warming stays below 5 °C
questions.explanation: Cutting emissions sooner slows warming, giving societies and ecosystems time to adapt, and limits the final temperature rise, which determines the scale of impacts and the risk of irreversible changes.

questions.stem: Under the Paris Agreement of 2015, countries agreed to hold warming to:
options: zero warming by cutting all emissions within five years
below 4 °C, with no requirement for national targets
well below 2 °C above pre-industrial, pursuing 1.5 °C
exactly 3 °C above pre-industrial levels by the year 2100
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement's goal is to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Each country sets its own nationally determined contribution and updates it every five years.

questions.stem: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), agreed in 1992, is important because it:
options: set up the framework for yearly climate negotiations
set binding emissions targets for every country from that year
banned the use of coal in all member countries from 1992
created the World Meteorological Organization to record weather
questions.explanation: The UNFCCC created the process, including the yearly Conferences of the Parties, under which the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement were later negotiated. Binding targets for developed countries came with Kyoto in 1997.

questions.stem: A city council installs solar panels on its buildings, plants street trees for shade and updates flood maps for rising seas. This shows climate action at which scale?
options: local, mixing mitigation and adaptation
global, through an international treaty
national, through federal legislation
household, through personal choices only
questions.explanation: Local governments act on both emissions (solar) and impacts (shade, flood planning). Action happens at every scale, from individuals to international agreements.

questions.stem: Which is an example of innovation helping to reduce climate risk?
options: removing sea walls and flood levees from low-lying towns
early-warning systems linking satellites and phone alerts
building more coal-fired power stations near large cities
draining coastal wetlands to make room for housing
questions.explanation: New technologies such as satellite monitoring and mobile alerts give people more time to prepare for heatwaves, cyclones and floods, building resilience.

questions.stem: Resilience in the context of climate change refers to the ability of a community to:
options: avoid every impact by moving to another country
deny that climate change is affecting its region
anticipate, absorb and recover from climate shocks
stop all climate change in its local area by itself
questions.explanation: Resilient communities prepare for, cope with and bounce back from events such as floods and heatwaves, and adapt to longer-term changes.

questions.stem: More frequent and intense heatwaves are a major climate change impact on people in Australian cities. Which group is generally most vulnerable?
options: residents of cool coastal suburbs with large shady gardens
older people and those with chronic illness or poor housing
young adults living in air-conditioned, well-insulated homes
office workers in the central business district during winter
questions.explanation: Heat stress harms people whose bodies cope less well or who cannot keep cool, such as the elderly, the chronically ill and those in poorly insulated housing. Heat is Australia's deadliest natural hazard.

questions.stem: Which is an example of national-scale climate change mitigation?
options: a farmer planting a windbreak to shade livestock during heatwaves
an international treaty negotiated among nearly 200 countries
a government scheme that sets emissions limits for large industrial facilities
a family installing a rainwater tank to cope with drier summers
questions.explanation: National policies such as emissions limits on large emitters, renewable energy targets or carbon pricing reduce emissions across a country. A treaty is global action, and the household and farm actions are adaptation.

questions.stem: Tuvalu has reclaimed and raised land on its main atoll, Funafuti, as part of a coastal adaptation project. This response mainly aims to:
options: create higher land above storm wave and flood levels
reduce Tuvalu's greenhouse gas emissions to zero
move the whole population to another country at once
increase the amount of coral reef around the atoll
questions.explanation: Raised, reclaimed land gives space for homes and infrastructure above projected flood levels. It is adaptation, as Tuvalu's own emissions are tiny.

questions.stem: Under the Falepili Union announced in 2023, Australia offered a special pathway for up to 280 Tuvaluans each year to live in Australia. In managing climate change, this is best described as:
options: a plan to move every Tuvaluan to Australia within a year
a treaty that requires Tuvalu to stop all coastal works
a migration option giving people choice as risks grow
a mitigation policy that cuts Australia's emissions
questions.explanation: Mobility pathways allow people to move with dignity if they choose, alongside adaptation at home. They do not reduce emissions or force relocation.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest limitation on how effectively Tuvalu can manage sea level rise on its own?
options: sea level around Tuvalu is falling, so no action is needed
its future depends on global emissions cuts
it has too much high land to make adaptation worthwhile
it produces most of the world's greenhouse gas emissions
questions.explanation: Tuvalu can adapt locally, but the amount of sea level rise depends on how fast the world cuts emissions. Effective management needs both local adaptation and global mitigation.

questions.stem: A student compares adaptation to sea level rise in Tuvalu with that in the Netherlands, which has extensive dykes and storm-surge barriers. What best explains the difference in their options?
options: the Netherlands is not affected by rising sea levels
Tuvalu has no coastline exposed to the open ocean
both countries have identical resources and risks
differences in wealth, land and technical capacity
questions.explanation: Wealthier countries can afford large engineering works, while small island states have limited land, funds and expertise and rely more on international support. Lessons can still transfer between contexts.

questions.stem: Which indicator would best show whether a climate adaptation project on a low-lying island is effective over time?
options: the amount of rainfall recorded in a single month
the height of the tallest building on the island
fewer homes flooded during king tides and storms
the number of tourists visiting the island each year
questions.explanation: Adaptation succeeds if it reduces harm, such as flooding of homes and saltwater intrusion, measured over years that include extreme events.
